title: Interpret a probability as a long-run proportion
stem: A phone manufacturer's records over many thousands of phones show that 3% have a defective screen. A store receives a random shipment of 200 phones. The store manager says, "Since 3% are defective, exactly 6 phones in this shipment will have a defective screen." Which statement best evaluates the manager's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 3% of 200 is 6.
choices.rationale: This confuses an expected count (3% of 200 = 6) with a guaranteed count; the actual number in one shipment varies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because the manager should have used 97%, since most phones in the shipment are not defective.
choices.rationale: This confuses the event with its complement; 97% describes phones that are not defective and does not address the manager's claim of exactly 6.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because a 3% rate applies only to shipments of 1,000 or more phones.
choices.rationale: This invents a minimum shipment size; the 3% rate applies to every phone, so it applies to a shipment of 200.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because a probability describes the long-run proportion, so the number of defective phones in this particular shipment will vary around 6 and need not equal 6.
choices.rationale: Correct: 3% is a long-run proportion, so the number of defective phones in one shipment of 200 varies around 6 and need not equal 6.

title: Complement rule with dice and coins
stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two dice is at least 4?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is P(sum < 4) = 3/36 = 1/12, the complement; the question asks for sums of at least 4, which is 1 − 1/12.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This counts a sum of 4 as excluded too (6 outcomes), so it finds P(sum > 4) = 30/36 = 5/6 instead of P(sum ≥ 4).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This treats sums above and below the cutoff as equally likely, but the 36 outcomes are not split evenly.

title: Mutually exclusive versus independent from probabilities
stem: For two events A and B, P(A) = 0.50, P(B) = 0.30, and P(A or B) = 0.65. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, because P(A and B) = 0.15 > 0, but they are independent, because 0.15 = (0.50)(0.30).
choices.rationale: Correct: P(A and B) = 0.50 + 0.30 − 0.65 = 0.15 > 0, so the events are not mutually exclusive; 0.15 = (0.50)(0.30), so they are independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because P(A or B) = 0.65 is less than 1.
choices.rationale: A union below 1 says nothing about whether the events overlap; here P(A and B) = 0.15 > 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are both mutually exclusive and independent, because P(A and B) equals P(A)P(B).
choices.rationale: Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities can never be independent, and these events are not mutually exclusive anyway because P(A and B) = 0.15.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are neither mutually exclusive nor independent, because P(A or B) ≠ P(A) + P(B).
choices.rationale: P(A or B) ≠ P(A) + P(B) shows the events overlap, not that they are dependent; independence requires P(A and B) = P(A)P(B), which holds here.

title: Addition rule with overlap, then the complement
stem: At a school, 55% of students take Spanish, 30% take French, and 10% take both. What is the probability that a randomly selected student takes neither language?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This ignores the overlap: it adds 0.55 + 0.30 = 0.85 and takes 1 − 0.85, double counting students who take both.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This adds the overlap (0.55 + 0.30 + 0.10 = 0.95) instead of subtracting it.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This removes only the Spanish students (1 − 0.55) and forgets French students.

title: Independence from a two-way table
stem:
Two hundred students were classified by whether they play a school sport and whether they are on the honor roll.
Athlete, On honor roll: 24
Athlete, Not on honor roll: 56
Not an athlete, On honor roll: 36
Not an athlete, Not on honor roll: 84
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Being an athlete and being on the honor roll are independent, because P(honor roll | athlete) = 24/80 = 0.30 equals P(honor roll) = 60/200 = 0.30.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(athlete) = 0.40, P(honor roll) = 0.30 and P(both) = 24/200 = 0.12 = (0.40)(0.30), so the variables are independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Being an athlete and being on the honor roll are not independent, because more non-athletes (36) than athletes (24) are on the honor roll.
choices.rationale: This compares counts of unequal groups; independence must be judged from proportions within each group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Being an athlete and being on the honor roll are not independent, because P(athlete | honor roll) = 0.40 is not equal to P(honor roll | athlete) = 0.30.
choices.rationale: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different quantities; they need not be equal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Being an athlete and being on the honor roll are independent, because P(athlete and honor roll) = 0.12 is smaller than both P(athlete) and P(honor roll).
choices.rationale: A joint probability is always smaller than each marginal probability, so being smaller does not show independence.

title: Two draws without replacement
stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement. What is the probability that both marbles are the same color?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses replacement, (5/8)² + (3/8)² = 34/64 = 17/32, but the draws are made without replacement.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This counts only two red marbles, (5/8)(4/7) = 5/14, and misses two blue marbles.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: P(red then blue) = (5/8)(3/7), a different-colors outcome.

title: Interpret a probability as a long-run proportion (variant 1)
stem: A hospital's records over many years show that 12% of scheduled patients miss their appointment. Tomorrow 300 patients are scheduled. The scheduler says, "Exactly 36 patients will miss their appointment." Which statement best evaluates this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 12% of 300 is 36.
choices.rationale: Treats the expected count (12% of 300 = 36) as a guaranteed count.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because 12% is a long-run proportion, so the number who miss tomorrow will vary around 36 and need not equal 36.
choices.rationale: Correct: 12% is a long-run proportion, so the number of missed appointments out of 300 varies around 36 and need not equal 36.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because the scheduler should have used 88%, since most patients attend.
choices.rationale: Confuses the event with its complement; 88% describes attendance and does not address why the claim of exactly 36 is wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because a 12% rate applies only to clinics with at least 1,000 appointments in a day.
choices.rationale: Invents a minimum number of appointments; a long-run rate applies to every individual appointment.

title: Interpret a probability as a long-run proportion (variant 2)
stem: A seed company reports that, over many tests, 90% of its tomato seeds germinate. A gardener plants 20 seeds. Which statement is the most reasonable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 18 seeds are likely to germinate, but the actual number will vary from garden to garden.
choices.rationale: Correct: 90% of 20 is 18, which is the expected count, but the actual number germinating varies from garden to garden.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exactly 18 seeds will germinate, because 90% of 20 is 18.
choices.rationale: Treats the expected count (18) as guaranteed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least 18 seeds will germinate, because 90% is the minimum germination rate.
choices.rationale: Reads 90% as a minimum; it is a long-run average rate, so a garden can fall below 18.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing can be said about how many will germinate, because only 20 seeds are planted.
choices.rationale: A small sample still has an expected count (0.90 × 20 = 18); it simply varies more than a large sample would.

title: Interpret a probability as a long-run proportion (variant 3)
stem: A streaming service finds that, over millions of plays, 2% of videos stall at least once. An engineer tests 500 plays and says, "Since 2% stall, exactly 10 of these 500 plays will stall." Which statement best evaluates the engineer's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because 2% is too small a probability to apply to 500 plays.
choices.rationale: A small probability still applies to each play; 2% is not too small to apply to 500 plays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 2% of 500 is 10.
choices.rationale: Treats the expected count (2% of 500 = 10) as guaranteed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because a probability is a long-run proportion, so the number of stalls in these 500 plays will vary around 10 and need not equal 10.
choices.rationale: Correct: 2% is a long-run proportion, so the number of stalls in 500 plays varies around 10 and need not equal 10.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because the engineer should have used 98%, the probability that a play does not stall.
choices.rationale: Uses the complement; 98% is the chance a play does not stall and is not the issue with the claim.

title: Complement rule with dice and coins (variant 1)
stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 5?

title: Complement rule with dice and coins (variant 2)
stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one die shows a number greater than 1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the probability of the complementary event, not of the event the question asks about.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is the probability that both dice show more than 1, (5/6)² = 25/36; the question asks for at least one die above 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: the only outcome with no die above 1 is (1,1), so 1 − 1/36 = 35/36.

choices.label: D

title: Complement rule with dice and coins (variant 3)
stem: A fair coin is flipped 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one tail?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the probability of the complementary event, not of the event the question asks about.

choices.label: D

title: Mutually exclusive versus independent from probabilities (variant 1)
stem: At a high school, let C be the event that a randomly chosen student is in a club and J the event that the student has a job. P(C) = 0.40, P(J) = 0.25, and P(C or J) = 0.55. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C and J are mutually exclusive, because P(C or J) = 0.55 is less than 1.
choices.rationale: A union below 1 says nothing about overlap; P(C and J) = 0.10 > 0, so the events are not mutually exclusive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: C and J are not mutually exclusive, because P(C and J) = 0.10 > 0, but they are independent, because 0.10 = (0.40)(0.25).
choices.rationale: Correct: P(C and J) = 0.40 + 0.25 − 0.55 = 0.10 > 0, so the events are not mutually exclusive; 0.10 = (0.40)(0.25), so they are independent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: C and J are mutually exclusive and independent, because P(C and J) equals P(C)P(J).
choices.rationale: Mutually exclusive events have P(A and B) = 0; here P(C and J) = 0.10, so they overlap.

choices.label: D
choices.text: C and J are neither mutually exclusive nor independent, because P(C or J) ≠ P(C) + P(J).
choices.rationale: P(C or J) differing from P(C) + P(J) shows overlap, not dependence; independence is tested with P(C)P(J) = P(C and J).

title: Mutually exclusive versus independent from probabilities (variant 2)
stem: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.35, P(B) = 0.40, and P(A or B) = 0.75. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, because P(A) + P(B) = 0.75 is less than 1.
choices.rationale: A sum of probabilities under 1 does not show that the events overlap; here P(A and B) = 0, so they are mutually exclusive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because P(A and B) = 0, but they are not independent, because P(A)P(B) = 0.14 ≠ 0.
choices.rationale: Correct: 0.35 + 0.40 − 0.75 = 0, so the events are mutually exclusive; (0.35)(0.40) = 0.14 ≠ 0, so they are not independent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive and independent, because P(A and B) = 0 means one event does not affect the other.
choices.rationale: This confuses mutually exclusive with independent; mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities strongly affect each other, because one happening rules out the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are independent, because P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
choices.rationale: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) is the exclusivity condition, not independence.

title: Mutually exclusive versus independent from probabilities (variant 3)
stem: For two events A and B, P(A) = 0.60, P(B) = 0.50, and P(A or B) = 0.85. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because P(A or B) < P(A) + P(B).
choices.rationale: P(A or B) < P(A) + P(B) shows the events overlap, which means they are not mutually exclusive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are independent, because P(A or B) = 0.85 is greater than both P(A) and P(B).
choices.rationale: A union larger than each single probability is true of almost any pair of events and does not show independence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, because P(A and B) = 0.25 > 0, and they are not independent, because P(A)P(B) = 0.30 ≠ 0.25.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(A and B) = 0.60 + 0.50 − 0.85 = 0.25 > 0, so not mutually exclusive; 0.25 ≠ (0.60)(0.50) = 0.30, so not independent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, but they are independent, because P(A and B) = 0.25 is positive.
choices.rationale: Independence requires P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.30; here P(A and B) = 0.25, so they are dependent even though they overlap.

title: Addition rule with overlap, then the complement (variant 1)
stem: A survey of commuters finds that 45% bike to work, 25% take the bus, and 10% do both on different days. What is the probability that a randomly selected commuter does neither?

choices.rationale: This removes only the commuters who bike (1 − 0.45) and forgets those who take the bus.

title: Addition rule with overlap, then the complement (variant 2)
stem: Among adults in a town, 38% read news online, 27% read a print paper, and 9% do both. What is the probability that a randomly selected adult reads neither?

title: Addition rule with overlap, then the complement (variant 3)
stem: Of 200 students, 90 play soccer, 70 play basketball, and 30 play both. What is the probability that a randomly selected student plays neither sport?

choices.label: A

title: Independence from a two-way table (variant 1)
stem:
A company classified 250 workers by work location and whether they completed an optional training.
Remote, Completed: 45
Remote, Did not complete: 55
On-site, Completed: 30
On-site, Did not complete: 120
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Work location and completing the training are independent, because both groups have more workers who did not complete than who did.
choices.rationale: Counts of unequal groups cannot be compared; the right comparison is within-group proportions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Work location and completing the training are not independent, because P(completed | remote) = 45/100 = 0.45 is not equal to P(completed) = 75/250 = 0.30.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(completed | remote) = 45/100 = 0.45 differs from P(completed) = 75/250 = 0.30, so the variables are not independent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Work location and completing the training are independent, because P(remote and completed) = 0.18 is smaller than both P(remote) and P(completed).
choices.rationale: A joint probability is always smaller than each marginal probability, so being smaller does not show independence; here the conditional proportions differ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Work location and completing the training are not independent, because P(remote | completed) = 0.60 is not equal to P(completed | remote) = 0.45.
choices.rationale: P(remote | completed) and P(completed | remote) are different quantities that are allowed to differ even when the variables are independent.

title: Independence from a two-way table (variant 2)
stem:
Three hundred students were classified by grade and by whether they take an AP class.
Senior, Take AP: 48
Senior, No AP: 72
Junior, Take AP: 72
Junior, No AP: 108
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grade and taking an AP class are not independent, because more juniors (72) than seniors (48) take an AP class.
choices.rationale: Compares counts of unequal groups; independence is judged from proportions, and 40% of both seniors and juniors take AP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grade and taking an AP class are not independent, because P(junior | AP) = 0.60 is not equal to P(senior | AP) = 0.40.
choices.rationale: P(junior | AP) and P(senior | AP) describe the same group split two ways and always differ; they do not test independence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grade and taking an AP class are independent, because P(senior and AP) = 0.16 is smaller than both P(senior) and P(AP).
choices.rationale: A joint probability is always smaller than each marginal probability, so this does not show independence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grade and taking an AP class are independent, because P(AP | senior) = 48/120 = 0.40 equals P(AP) = 120/300 = 0.40.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(AP | senior) = 48/120 = 0.40 equals P(AP) = 120/300 = 0.40, so the variables are independent.

title: Independence from a two-way table (variant 3)
stem:

choices.text: Membership and buying on sale are not independent, because P(bought on sale | member) = 72/160 = 0.45 is not equal to P(bought on sale) = 120/400 = 0.30.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(bought on sale | member) = 72/160 = 0.45 differs from P(bought on sale) = 120/400 = 0.30, so the variables are not independent.

choices.text: Membership and buying on sale are not independent, because P(member | bought on sale) = 0.60 is not equal to P(bought on sale | member) = 0.45.

choices.rationale: This uses only server 1; with a second server the chance that at least one responds is higher.

title: At least one of several independent events (variant 2)
stem: A security system uses three independent sensors. Each sensor detects an intruder with probability 0.70. What is the probability that at least one sensor detects the intruder?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the probability that all three sensors detect, 0.7³; the question asks for at least one.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is the probability that exactly one sensor detects; at least one also includes two or three detecting.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the probability for a single sensor; with three sensors the chance that at least one detects is higher.

title: At least one of several independent events (variant 3)
stem: Ana makes a free throw with probability 0.60 and Ben with probability 0.50. Each takes one shot, independently. What is the probability that at least one of them makes the shot?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the probability that both players make the shot, (0.60)(0.50); the question asks for at least one.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This averages the two probabilities, which is not a valid way to combine independent events.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the probability that exactly one player makes the shot; at least one also includes the case that both make it.

title: Mean and SD after a linear change Y = aX + b
stem: A random variable X has mean 4 and standard deviation 1.5. Let Y = 3X − 2. What are the mean and standard deviation of Y?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean 10, standard deviation 4.5

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean 10, standard deviation 2.5
choices.rationale: This subtracts 2 from the SD; adding or subtracting a constant shifts the mean but does not change the SD.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean 12, standard deviation 4.5
choices.rationale: This forgets the −2: the mean of Y is 3(4) − 2 = 10, not 3(4).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean 10, standard deviation 13.5
choices.rationale: This multiplies the SD by 9 (the square of 3); the SD is multiplied by 3, and only the variance by 9.

title: Mean and SD after a linear change Y = aX + b (variant 1)
stem: A random variable X has mean 20 and standard deviation 4. Let Y = 0.5X + 10. What are the mean and standard deviation of Y?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean 20, standard deviation 12
choices.rationale: This adds 10 to the SD; a constant added to every value shifts the mean but does not change the SD.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean 20, standard deviation 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean 20, standard deviation 4
choices.rationale: Multiplying a random variable by a constant multiplies its standard deviation by that constant, so the SD does not stay unscaled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean 30, standard deviation 2
choices.rationale: This adds 10 to the original mean without scaling it by 0.5 first.

title: Mean and SD after a linear change Y = aX + b (variant 2)
stem: The number of items X in an online order has mean 3.2 and standard deviation 1.1. A shipping charge is C = 4 + 2.5X dollars. What are the mean and standard deviation of C?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean $8, standard deviation $2.75
choices.rationale: This forgets the $4 base fee: the mean of C is 4 + 2.5(3.2) = 12, not 2.5(3.2) = 8.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean $12, standard deviation $6.75
choices.rationale: This adds the $4 base fee to the SD; a constant added to every value shifts the mean but does not change the SD.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean $12, standard deviation $1.10
choices.rationale: Multiplying a random variable by a constant multiplies its standard deviation by that constant, so the SD does not stay unscaled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean $12, standard deviation $2.75

title: Mean and SD after a linear change Y = aX + b (variant 3)
stem: A random variable X has mean 15 and standard deviation 3. Let Y = 50 − 2X. What are the mean and standard deviation of Y?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean 20, standard deviation 6

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean 20, standard deviation −6
choices.rationale: A standard deviation cannot be negative; multiplying by −2 multiplies the SD by |−2| = 2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean 80, standard deviation 6
choices.rationale: This adds 2(15) to 50 instead of subtracting it; Y = 50 − 2X, so the mean is 50 − 2(15) = 20.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean 20, standard deviation 3
choices.rationale: Multiplying a random variable by a constant multiplies its standard deviation by that constant, so the SD does not stay unscaled.

title: Expected net gain with a cost
stem: A charity sells 400 raffle tickets at $10 each. There is one grand prize of $1,000 and three prizes of $200. What is the expected net gain for a person who buys one ticket?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This leaves out the $10 ticket price; the expected prize is $4, but the net gain is 4 − 10.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This counts only the $1,000 grand prize (expected $2.50) and leaves out the three $200 prizes.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This assumes the whole $10 is lost; the prizes return an expected $4 per ticket, so the net is −$6.

title: Expected net gain with a cost (variant 1)
stem: A school fair sells 500 tickets at $4 each. There is one prize of $600 and two prizes of $100. What is the expected net gain for a person who buys one ticket?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This leaves out the $4 ticket price; the expected prize is $1.60, but the net gain is 1.60 − 4.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: expected prize (600 + 200)/500 = 1.60; net 1.60 − 4 = −2.40.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This counts only the $600 prize (expected $1.20) and leaves out the two $100 prizes.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Treats the ticket price as simply lost; the winnings reduce that loss.

title: Expected net gain with a cost (variant 2)
stem: A carnival game costs $5 to play. A fair six-sided die is rolled: a 6 pays $12, a 5 pays $6, and any other roll pays $0. What is the expected net gain per play?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This leaves out the $5 cost; the expected payout is $3, but the net gain is 3 − 5.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: expected payout 12(1/6) + 6(1/6) = 3.00; net 3.00 − 5 = −2.00.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This counts only the $12 prize (expected $2) and leaves out the $6 prize.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Treats the $5 cost as the net result and ignores the expected $3 payout.

title: Expected net gain with a cost (variant 3)
stem: An insurance company charges a $120 premium. With probability 0.10 it pays a $500 claim, with probability 0.02 it pays a $2,000 claim, and otherwise it pays nothing. What is the company's expected profit per policy?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the company's expected payout ($90), not its profit; profit is the $120 premium minus the payout.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This has the sign reversed; the company's profit is the premium minus the payout, 120 − 90 = $30.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This counts only the $500 claims (expected $50) and leaves out the $2,000 claims.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: expected payout 0.10(500) + 0.02(2,000) = 90; profit 120 − 90 = 30.

title: Is sampling without replacement approximately binomial
stem: In a large school of 1,800 students, 10% are left-handed. A teacher randomly selects 25 students, and X is the number who are left-handed. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X is not binomial, because the students are selected without replacement.
choices.rationale: Sampling without replacement does not make X non-binomial here: a sample of 25 from 1,800 students is small enough that the trials are nearly independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: X is approximately binomial, because the sample is a small fraction of the school, so the trials are nearly independent with nearly constant P(left-handed).
choices.rationale: Correct: 25 is a small fraction of 1,800, so the selections are nearly independent with P(left-handed) nearly constant at 0.10.

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is not binomial, because the probability of being left-handed, 0.10, is too small.
choices.rationale: A binomial setting has no minimum value for p; 0.10 is perfectly acceptable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: X is exactly binomial, because the number of trials is fixed at 25.
choices.rationale: A fixed number of trials is only one condition; the trials must also be independent with a constant probability, which holds only approximately here.

title: Is sampling without replacement approximately binomial (variant 1)
stem: A city has 5,000 registered voters, and 52% favor a ballot measure. A pollster randomly selects 50 voters, and X is the number who favor the measure. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X is binomial only if the pollster samples with replacement.
choices.rationale: Sampling without replacement from a large population is still approximately binomial; replacement is not required.

choices.label: B
choices.text: X is not binomial, because 0.52 is not equal to 0.50.
choices.rationale: A binomial probability does not need to equal 0.50; any constant p works.

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is approximately binomial, because 50 is a small fraction of 5,000, so the trials are nearly independent with P(favor) nearly constant at 0.52.
choices.rationale: Correct: 50 is a small fraction of 5,000, so the trials are nearly independent with P(favor) nearly constant at 0.52.

choices.label: D
choices.text: X is exactly binomial, because there are only two possible responses.
choices.rationale: Two possible responses is only one of the conditions; the trials must also be independent with constant probability.

title: Is sampling without replacement approximately binomial (variant 2)
stem: A class of 30 students includes 12 who are left-handed. A teacher randomly selects 10 students from the class without replacement, and X is the number who are left-handed. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X is binomial, because there are exactly 10 trials with two outcomes each.
choices.rationale: A fixed number of trials with two outcomes is not enough; the trials must also be independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: X is binomial, because the probability of selecting a left-handed student on the first pick is 12/30 = 0.40.
choices.rationale: The probability on the first pick is 0.40, but it changes after each pick without replacement from a small group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is not binomial, because the students can be left-handed or right-handed but not both.
choices.rationale: Having two categories is what a binomial setting requires, so this is not a reason the setting fails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: X is not approximately binomial, because the sample is one-third of the class, so each pick changes the probability for the next.
choices.rationale: Correct: 10 of 30 is a third of the class, so each pick changes the probability for the next and the trials are not approximately independent.

title: Is sampling without replacement approximately binomial (variant 3)
stem: A town has 12,000 residents, and 20% own an electric vehicle. A researcher randomly selects 30 residents, and X is the number who own an electric vehicle. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X is not binomial, because sampling without replacement always makes trials dependent.
choices.rationale: Sampling without replacement does not always break independence; with a small sample from a large population it is approximately binomial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: X is exactly binomial, because the number of residents sampled is fixed.
choices.rationale: A fixed number of trials is not enough by itself; independence and constant probability are also needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is approximately binomial, because 30 is a small fraction of 12,000, so P(owns an electric vehicle) stays nearly 0.20 on every pick.
choices.rationale: Correct: 30 is a small fraction of 12,000, so P(owns an electric vehicle) stays nearly 0.20 on every pick.

choices.label: D
choices.text: X is binomial only if 30 is at least half the town.
choices.rationale: There is no requirement that the sample be half the town; the opposite, a small sample, is what makes it approximately binomial.

title: Cumulative binomial probability (at least k)
stem: Each of 6 independent customers buys an upgrade with probability 0.25. Let X be the number who buy the upgrade. What is P(X ≥ 2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is P(X = 2) only; P(X ≥ 2) also includes 3, 4, 5 and 6 successes.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(0); the question asks for at least 2, so P(1) must also be subtracted.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≤ 1), the complement of the event asked about.

title: Cumulative binomial probability (at least k) (variant 1)
stem: Each of 8 independent seeds sprouts with probability 0.30. Let X be the number that sprout. What is P(X ≥ 2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is P(X = 2) only; P(X ≥ 2) includes every value from 2 to 8.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≥ 1); the question asks for at least 2, so P(1) must also be subtracted.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≤ 1), the complement of the event asked about.

title: Cumulative binomial probability (at least k) (variant 2)
stem: Each of 10 independent calls is answered with probability 0.20. Let X be the number answered. What is P(X ≥ 3)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is P(X = 3) only; P(X ≥ 3) includes every value from 3 to 10.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≤ 3), which includes the values the question excludes.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≥ 4); the boundary is off by one, because the question asks for at least 3.

title: Cumulative binomial probability (at least k) (variant 3)
stem: Each of 5 independent free throws is made with probability 0.40. Let X be the number made. What is P(X ≥ 4)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is P(X = 4) only; P(X ≥ 4) also includes P(X = 5).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≥ 3); the boundary is off by one, because the question asks for at least 4.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is P(X ≤ 4), which is nearly everything; the question asks for 4 or more.

title: Compare groups by within-group percent, not counts
stem:
A school surveyed 200 students about whether they prefer online meetings.
Freshman, Prefer online: 45
Freshman, Prefer in person: 15
Senior, Prefer online: 56
Senior, Prefer in person: 84
A student says, "More seniors (56) than freshmen (45) prefer online, so seniors are more likely to prefer online." Which is the best evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 56 is greater than 45.
choices.rationale: Compares counts of groups of different sizes; there are far more seniors, so more seniors can prefer online even if a smaller share does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 56/200 = 28% of all students are seniors who prefer online, compared with 45/200 = 22.5% for freshmen.
choices.rationale: Uses the percent of all 200 students, which still depends on group size; the fair comparison is within each group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because the groups differ in size: 45/60 = 75% of freshmen prefer online, compared with 56/140 = 40% of seniors.
choices.rationale: Correct: 45/60 = 75% of freshmen prefer online, compared with 56/140 = 40% of seniors, so freshmen are more likely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because 101 of the 200 students prefer online, which is more than half.
choices.rationale: The overall rate (101/200) does not say which group is more likely to prefer online.

title: Compare groups by within-group percent, not counts (variant 1)
stem:
A club coordinator recorded whether 250 members attended weekend events.
Art Club, Attended: 60
Art Club, Did not attend: 20
Chess Club, Attended: 85
Chess Club, Did not attend: 85
A member says, "More Chess Club members (85) than Art Club members (60) attended, so Chess Club members are more likely to attend." Which is the best evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because the clubs differ in size: 60/80 = 75% of Art Club members attended, compared with 85/170 = 50% of Chess Club members.
choices.rationale: Correct: 60/80 = 75% of Art Club members attended, compared with 85/170 = 50% of Chess Club members.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 85 is greater than 60.
choices.rationale: Compares counts of clubs of different sizes; Chess Club is more than twice as large.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because 145 of the 250 members attended, which is more than half.
choices.rationale: The overall attendance rate (145/250) does not compare the two clubs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 85/250 = 34% of all members are Chess Club attendees, compared with 60/250 = 24% for Art Club.
choices.rationale: Uses the percent of all 250 members, which depends on group size; the fair comparison is within each club.

title: Compare groups by within-group percent, not counts (variant 2)
stem:
A survey of 300 commuters recorded where they live and whether they use transit weekly.
Urban, Use transit: 130
Urban, Do not: 70
Rural, Use transit: 20
Rural, Do not: 80
A reporter says, "Urban residents are more likely to use transit, because 130 urban residents do, compared with only 20 rural residents." Which is the best evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is wrong, because the group counts cannot be compared at all, so no conclusion is possible.
choices.rationale: Group counts can be compared once they are converted to within-group percentages, so a conclusion is possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 130 is greater than 20, which shows urban residents are more likely.
choices.rationale: The conclusion happens to be right, but a larger count alone is not valid evidence when the groups differ in size.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conclusion is correct, but the reasoning should compare percentages within each group: 130/200 = 65% of urban residents versus 20/100 = 20% of rural residents.
choices.rationale: Correct: the conclusion holds (65% of urban versus 20% of rural), but the support for it should be the within-group percentages, not the raw counts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because 150 of the 300 commuters use transit, which is exactly half.
choices.rationale: The overall rate of 150/300 does not compare urban and rural residents.

title: Compare groups by within-group percent, not counts (variant 3)
stem:
A gym has 300 members: 200 are over 40 and 100 are 40 or under. Members were asked whether they use the gym's app.
Over 40, Use app: 65
Over 40, Do not: 135
40 or under, Use app: 55
40 or under, Do not: 45
A manager says, "About 54% of app users are over 40, so members over 40 are more likely to use the app." Which is the best evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 54% is greater than 50%.
choices.rationale: A share above 50% of app users is meaningless without comparing it with the group's share of all members.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because 65 over-40 members use the app, compared with 55 members who are 40 or under.
choices.rationale: Compares counts of unequal groups; there are twice as many over-40 members.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is incorrect, because only 120 of the 300 members, or 40%, use the app.
choices.rationale: The overall app-use rate (40%) does not compare the two age groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect: over-40 members are 200/300 ≈ 67% of all members, so 54% of app users is below their share; within groups, 65/200 = 32.5% of over-40 members use the app versus 55/100 = 55% of the others.
choices.rationale: Correct: over-40 members are about 67% of all members, so 54% of app users is below their share; within groups, 32.5% of over-40 members use the app versus 55% of the others.

title: Choose a display for groups of different sizes
stem: A researcher surveys 1,000 commuters in four cities with very different populations (the smallest sample is 50 people and the largest is 600). Each person reports whether they usually commute by car, transit, or bike. The researcher wants to compare commuting patterns across the four cities. Which display is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single pie chart of all 1,000 responses.
choices.rationale: A single pie chart of all 1,000 responses combines the cities and hides the comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A bar chart of the number of people surveyed in each city.
choices.rationale: Showing only how many were surveyed in each city says nothing about commuting patterns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A segmented bar graph showing, for each city, the percent of that city's respondents using each commuting mode.
choices.rationale: Correct: a segmented bar graph of within-city percents puts the four cities on a common scale despite very different sample sizes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A side-by-side bar graph showing the number of people using each mode in each city.
choices.rationale: Counts are not comparable across cities of very different sizes; the larger cities will dominate regardless of pattern.

title: Choose a display for groups of different sizes (variant 1)
stem: A coach records the position (guard, forward, center) played by students on three school teams of very different sizes and wants to compare position patterns across the teams. Which display is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A segmented bar graph of the percent of each team's students at each position.
choices.rationale: Correct: percents within each team put teams of very different sizes on a common scale.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A bar chart of the number of students on each team.
choices.rationale: The number of students on each team says nothing about the positions played.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pie chart of all students' positions combined.
choices.rationale: A combined pie chart hides differences between the teams.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A side-by-side bar graph of the number of students at each position on each team.
choices.rationale: Counts of positions are not comparable across teams of very different sizes.

title: Choose a display for groups of different sizes (variant 2)
stem: An inspector samples items from three factories that produce very different volumes and records whether each item is acceptable, minor defect, or major defect. The inspector wants to see whether the defect pattern differs by factory. Which display is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A segmented bar graph of the percent of each factory's sampled items in each defect category.
choices.rationale: Correct: percents within each factory put factories of very different volumes on a common scale.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pie chart of the defect types for all sampled items combined.
choices.rationale: A combined pie chart hides differences between the factories.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bar chart of the number of items sampled from each factory.
choices.rationale: The number sampled from each factory says nothing about defect patterns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A side-by-side bar graph of the number of items in each defect category for each factory.
choices.rationale: Counts of defects are not comparable across factories of very different volumes.

title: Choose a display for groups of different sizes (variant 3)
stem: A segmented bar graph shows, for each of four age groups, the percent who prefer each of three streaming services. If the two variables (age group and service preference) are not associated, what would the graph show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The segments would be split in nearly the same proportions in every bar.
choices.rationale: Correct: if the variables are not associated, the distribution of service preference is nearly the same within every age group, so every bar is split in about the same proportions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four bars of equal height, each split into three equal segments.
choices.rationale: In a segmented bar graph of percents every bar is the same height (100%), but equal splits of exactly one third are not required for no association.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The segments in each bar would be the same size as the group's sample size.
choices.rationale: Segment size reflects a percent of the group, not the group's sample size.

choices.label: D
choices.text: One service would take up the largest segment in exactly one of the bars.
choices.rationale: One segment being largest in only one bar would indicate that the distribution differs by group, which suggests association.

title: Association from conditional proportions in a two-way table
stem:
In a clinical study of 500 patients, 200 received Treatment A and 300 received Treatment B.
Treatment A, Recovered: 120
Treatment A, Did not recover: 80
Treatment B, Recovered: 120
Treatment B, Did not recover: 180
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is no association, because the same number of patients (120) recovered under each treatment.
choices.rationale: Equal counts of recovered patients do not mean equal rates when the groups have different sizes (200 versus 300).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Treatment B has the higher recovery rate, because more patients received B (300) than A (200).
choices.rationale: Group size does not determine the recovery rate; B has more patients but a lower rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The recovery rate is 48% for both treatments, because 240/500 = 0.48.
choices.rationale: 48% is the overall recovery rate and hides the difference between the treatments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is an association: 120/200 = 60% of patients on A recovered, compared with 120/300 = 40% on B.
choices.rationale: Correct: 120/200 = 60% of patients on A recovered versus 120/300 = 40% on B, so recovery differs by treatment.

title: Association from conditional proportions in a two-way table (variant 1)
stem:
A school tracked 400 students: 150 used tutoring and 250 did not.
Tutoring, Passed: 105
Tutoring, Did not pass: 45
No tutoring, Passed: 125
No tutoring, Did not pass: 125
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tutoring does not help, because more students passed without tutoring (125) than with it (105).
choices.rationale: Compares counts of groups of different sizes; the tutored group is smaller but has the higher pass rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is an association: 105/150 = 70% of tutored students passed, compared with 125/250 = 50% of the others.
choices.rationale: Correct: 105/150 = 70% of tutored students passed versus 125/250 = 50% of the others.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pass rate is 57.5% for both groups, because 230/400 = 0.575.
choices.rationale: 57.5% is the overall pass rate and hides the difference between the two groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no association, because 105 and 125 are close.
choices.rationale: Close counts (105 and 125) do not mean close rates; the groups have different sizes.

title: Association from conditional proportions in a two-way table (variant 2)
stem:
A delivery company recorded 500 deliveries by area and whether the delivery was late.
City, Late: 90
City, On time: 210
Suburb, Late: 60
Suburb, On time: 140
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is an association, because more city deliveries (90) than suburb deliveries (60) were late.
choices.rationale: More late deliveries in the city (90 versus 60) reflects its larger volume, not a higher late rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The suburb has the lower late rate, because it has fewer deliveries.
choices.rationale: Having fewer deliveries does not make a late rate lower; the rates are equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lateness is related to area, because 150 of the 500 deliveries were late.
choices.rationale: The overall late rate (30%) matches each group's rate, which shows no relationship, not one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no association in these data: 90/300 = 30% of city deliveries and 60/200 = 30% of suburb deliveries were late.
choices.rationale: Correct: 90/300 = 30% of city and 60/200 = 30% of suburb deliveries were late, so lateness is not associated with area here.

title: Association from conditional proportions in a two-way table (variant 3)
stem:
A health app study followed 300 adults: 180 used a sleep app and 120 did not.
Used app, Improved sleep: 72
Used app, Did not improve: 108
Did not use app, Improved sleep: 66
Did not use app, Did not improve: 54
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A

choices.text: There is no association, because 138/300 = 46% improved overall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is an association, and non-users did better: 66/120 = 55% of non-users improved, compared with 72/180 = 40% of app users.
choices.rationale: Correct: 66/120 = 55% of non-users improved versus 72/180 = 40% of app users, so non-users did better in these data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The app has no effect, because 72 and 66 are nearly equal.

title: Conditional probability from joint proportions
stem:
A survey classified adults by age group and phone type. The table shows the proportion of all adults in each category.
Under 30, iOS: 0.30
Under 30, Android: 0.20
30 or older, iOS: 0.15
30 or older, Android: 0.35
Among adults who use iOS, what proportion are under 30?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the joint proportion of the whole group for both categories, not the proportion within the group the question names.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is P(iOS), the proportion who use iOS, not the proportion of iOS users who are under 30.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is P(iOS | under 30) = 0.30/0.50, the proportion of under-30 adults who use iOS; the question asks for the reverse.

title: Conditional probability from joint proportions (variant 1)

stem:

title: Simulation design: waiting for the first success
stem: A cereal company puts a prize in 25% of its boxes, randomly and independently. A student plans to use a table of random digits to estimate the probability that it takes at least 4 boxes to get the first prize. Which simulation design is valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Let digits 0, 1 and 2 represent a prize. Read single digits until a prize appears, record the number of digits read, and repeat many times.
choices.rationale: Three of the ten digits is 30%, not 25%, so the simulated prize rate is wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Let two-digit numbers 01 to 25 represent a prize. One trial is reading two-digit numbers until a prize appears, recording the number of boxes; repeat many times and find the proportion of trials needing at least 4 boxes.
choices.rationale: Correct: 01 to 25 is exactly 25 of the 100 two-digit numbers, and a trial reads numbers until the first prize, so repeating many trials estimates the proportion needing at least 4 boxes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Let two-digit numbers 01 to 25 represent a prize. One trial is a single two-digit number. Do the trial 4 times and record the proportion of prizes.
choices.rationale: This estimates the proportion of boxes with a prize (about 25%), not the probability that it takes at least 4 boxes to get the first one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Let two-digit numbers 01 to 25 represent a prize. One trial is four two-digit numbers; record whether none of them is a prize; repeat many times.
choices.rationale: Recording "no prize in four boxes" estimates the chance of needing at least 5 boxes, not at least 4.

title: Simulation design: waiting for the first success (variant 1)
stem: A scratch-off game wins on 20% of tickets, randomly and independently. A student wants to estimate the probability that it takes at least 3 tickets to get the first winner, using random digits. Which design is valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Let digits 0, 1 and 2 represent a winner. Read digits until a winner appears, record the count, repeat many times.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Let digits 0 and 1 represent a winner. One trial is three digits; record whether none is a winner; repeat many times.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

choices.rationale: This estimates the proportion of tickets that win (about 20%), not the probability that it takes at least 3 tickets to get the first winner.

title: Simulation design: waiting for the first success (variant 2)
stem: A basketball player makes 40% of her shots, independently. A student wants to estimate the probability that she makes exactly 2 of her next 5 shots, using random digits. Which design is valid?

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Let digits 0 to 3 represent a made shot. One trial is five digits; record whether at least 2 are made; repeat many times.
choices.rationale: This records at least 2 made shots, but the question asks for exactly 2.

title: Simulation design: waiting for the first success (variant 3)
stem: The chance of rain on any day in a region is 35%, independently from day to day. A student wants to estimate the probability that it rains on exactly 2 of the next 3 days, using random digits. Which design is valid?

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Let two-digit numbers 00 to 34 represent rain. One trial is three numbers; record whether exactly 2 are rain; repeat many times.
choices.rationale: Correct: 00 to 34 is exactly 35 of the 100 two-digit numbers, and a trial of three numbers records whether exactly 2 are rain; repeating many trials estimates the probability.

title: Estimate and reliability from simulation results
stem:
A student simulates flipping a fair coin 5 times and records the number of heads, repeating this for 100 trials.
Heads = 0: 3 trials
Heads = 1: 15 trials
Heads = 2: 32 trials
Heads = 3: 30 trials
Heads = 4: 16 trials
Heads = 5: 4 trials
Based on this simulation, what is the estimated probability of at least 4 heads, and which statement about it is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.20; it is the exact probability, because 100 trials were used.
choices.rationale: Simulation results are estimates, not exact probabilities, regardless of how many trials are run.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.16; it is an estimate that would change in a new simulation, and more trials would make it more reliable.
choices.rationale: This is the estimate for exactly 4 heads (16/100), not for at least 4 heads, which also includes 5 heads.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.20; it is an estimate that would change in a new simulation, and more trials would make it more reliable.
choices.rationale: Correct: (16 + 4)/100 = 0.20; a simulation gives an estimate that changes from run to run and becomes more reliable with more trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.20; it is an estimate, and fewer trials would make it more reliable.
choices.rationale: Fewer trials make an estimate less reliable, not more.

title: Recognize a valid probability distribution (variant 3)

choices.label: D

title: How sample size changes the SD of the sample mean
stem: A population of delivery times has standard deviation 20 minutes. A researcher takes random samples and computes the sample mean. When the sample size is 25, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄ is 4 minutes. If the sample size is increased to 100, which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standard deviation of x̄ decreases from 4 to 2, because it is proportional to 1/√n.
choices.rationale: Correct: the standard deviation of x̄ is σ/√n, so it goes from 20/√25 = 4 to 20/√100 = 2.

choices.label: B

choices.rationale: Quadrupling n halves the standard deviation of x̄ (it depends on √n), it does not quarter it.

choices.label: D
